title: Wayfinding for People With Dementia: A Review of the Role of Architectural Design
review_question: To provide an overview of the available literature on architectural wayfinding design for people with dementia in nursing homes, summarize the results, and substantiate them through an interdisciplinary interpretation, taking into account changes in the orientation process of people with dementia.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Literature on architectural wayfinding design for people with dementia in nursing homes. Studies enrolling only people with Alzheimer's disease are noted. Focus on empirical evidence from nursing home settings.

synthesis_conclusions: Floor plan designs significantly support the spatial orientation and wayfinding of people with dementia.
Interventions such as signage, furnishings, lighting, and colors are supporting features but cannot compensate for an adverse architectural design.
For a supportive, dementia-friendly environment, both floor plan typology and environmental cues must be considered.

Design guidelines to support wayfinding abilities of people with dementia include: 1) no need for new or higher skills, 2) allow visual access and overview, 3) reduce decision making, and 4) increase architectural legibility.
evidence_gaps: Additional research is needed to better understand the relationship between architectural design and human behavior.
The operational requirements of nursing homes in relation to floor plan typologies of facilities need to be investigated.
heterogeneity_sources: The length of corridors, lighting intensity, architectural differentiation, natural light, views to the outside, and other sensory stimulation were not measured in studies comparing floor plan typologies, potentially explaining conflicting results.
limitations: The definitive diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease requires post-mortem examination, so most studies assume Alzheimer's type dementia based on clinical syndrome.

Conflicting results regarding straight corridors vs. L-shaped floor plans may be due to unmeasured variables like corridor length, lighting, architectural differentiation, natural light, and other sensory stimulation.

paper_metadata.title: A Framework for Immersive Virtual Environments (FIVE): Speculations on the Role of Presence in Virtual Environments
paper_metadata.crossref_title: A Framework for Immersive Virtual Environments (FIVE): Speculations on the Role of Presence in Virtual Environments
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This paper reviews the concepts of immersion and presence in virtual environments (VEs). We propose that the degree of immersion can be objectively assessed as the characteristics of a technology, and has dimensions such as the extent to which a display system can deliver an inclusive, extensive, surrounding, and vivid illusion of virtual environment to a participant. Other dimensions of immersion are concerned with the extent of body matching, and the extent to which there is a self-contained plot in which the participant can act and in which there is an autonomous response. Presence is a state of consciousness that may be concomitant with immersion, and is related to a sense of being in a place. Presence governs aspects of autonomie responses and higher-level behaviors of a participant in a VE. The paper considers single and multiparticipant shared environments, and draws on the experience of ComputerSupported Cooperative Working (CSCW) research as a guide to understanding presence in shared environments. The paper finally outlines the aims of the FIVE Working Group, and the 1995 FIVE Conference in London, UK.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Optimal wayfinding for people with dementia requires an environment where the level of environmental press (demands) is matched to their reduced cognitive competence.
Architectural design features influence the ability of individuals, particularly those with dementia, to form and utilize mental representations of space for navigation.

mechanism_chain.description: Architectural design of small-scale living units reduces environmental complexity and increases familiarity, thereby lowering cognitive load and improving spatial memory and recognition for wayfinding in people with dementia.
